The knowledge created at CERN helps mankind understand the fundamental laws of nature on the creation, evolution and the destiny of our Universe. It also develops new technologies for our society, such as the World Wide Web (WWW), etc., and serves as a training center for thousands of scientists and engineers for tomorrow. The United Nations and other international sectors have tried to learn from the

events.title: NFV(Network Function Virtualization) orchestration by Airship
events.body:
OpenStack has become the de-facto standard platform for running VNFs (Virtual Network Function). As network performance is key for many VNFs, OpenStack allows to utilize high-performance dataplanes, such as OpenVswitch with DPDK (OVS-DPDK). The Airship project builds tooling for deploying and managing OpenStack on Kubernetes by leveraging openstack-helm. Until recently, openstack-helm and Airship did not provide support for OVS-DPDK. So, we have made the effort to bring support for OVS-DPDK to openstack-helm and Airship.

In this session we are going to share how we enabled OVS-DPDK in Airship and demonstrate the end-to-end deployment flow of OVS-DPDK in Airship. Moreover, we will talk about the implementation details such as creating DPDK-enabled docker images for OVS, handling hugepage allocation for DPDK in openstack-helm and Kubernetes, CPU pinning, etc.
events.learning:
1. The use cases for OVS-DPDK in Airship

2. The technical details of our implementation in Airship and openstack-helm

3. End-to-end deployment of Airship airsloop in pure virtual env.

events.title: Machine Learning benchmarking with OpenStack and Kubernetes
events.body:
Deep Learning and Cloud Platforms are transforming the field of Machine Learning from theory to practice. However, implementation differences across frameworks and inference engines make the comparison of benchmark results difficult. SPEC and TPCC benchmarks are not accurate due to the complex interactions between implementation choices such as batch size, hyperparameters, or numerical precision. To address this complexity requires systematic benchmarking that is both representative of real-world use cases and valid across different software/hardware platforms.

This talk will present the best Machine Learning benchmarking tools to use with OpenStack and Kubernetes. We will show how MLPerf and Thoth help data scientists to improve their system performance and fully benefit from their CPUs, GPUs, or FPGAs. We will share insights and lessons learned over the journey of key Machine Learning training and inference use cases selection.

events.title: Reinventing Access Control: Access Rules in OpenStack Keystone

One of the core tenets of The Cloud is application-driven, self-service infrastructure management. Until now, OpenStack's system for managing access control has fundamentally hindered a true self-service user experience and required users to file tickets with their administrators in order to get their applications the access they need to do work. With the introduction of access rules for keystone application credentials, we can finally empower OpenStack users to take full control over their own cloud-native applications by delegating a minimal set of permissions to their applications without the need for operator interference.

events.title: Addressing the Challenge of Monitoring Edge Devices
events.body:
As we enter the era of Edge Computing, system operators will see a number of profound changes appear in their networks, both in the size of the networks that must be managed, and in the types of management operations that must be performed.

Rather than deploying thousands of hosts in a data center, edge clouds will deploy servers and other devices over thousands of different locations. New solutions must be found for providing scalable management and orchestration for edge clouds. 

The servers and devices will change in edge clouds. Servers may be deployed in harsh environments, and must consume telemetry, taking administrative actions autonomously. For example, an edge node may need to detect that its power level or environmental temp. are unsuitable for operation and proactively migrate applications elsewhere in the edge network. Edge nodes may be in environments with low levels of physical security and must be able to detect and respond to intrusions.

events.title: CERN OpenStack Cloud control plane: from VMs to K8s
events.body:
CERN is the home of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), a 27km circular proton accelerator that generates petabytes of physics data every year. To process all this data, CERN runs an OpenStack Cloud (>300K cores) that helps scientists all around the world to unveil the mysteries of the Universe. The Infrastructure is also used to run all the IT services of the Organization.

Delivering these services, with high performance and reliable service levels has been one of the major challenges for the CERN Cloud engineering team. We have been constantly iterating the architecture and deployment model of the Cloud control plane.

In this presentation we will describe the different control plane architecture models that we relied over the years. Finally, we will describe all the work done to move the OpenStack Cloud control plane from VMs into a kubernetes cluster. We will report about our experience running this architecture at scale, its advantages and challenges.
events.learning:
This presentation will describe how CERN is moving its OpenStack Cloud control plane from VMs to Kubernetes.

We will start with an overview about the CERN OpenStack Cloud. Then we will dive into the infrastructure architecture and describe the different architecture choices for the control plane.

Finally, we will describe all the work done to move the OpenStack Cloud control plane to a kubernetes cluster provisioned by Magnum and deployed in the same infrastructure, report about our experience running this setup at scale, its caveats and how we are mitigating them.

events.title: Rethinking Hyper-Converged Infrastructure for Edge Computing
events.body:
Due to the diversity of requires, solutions of Edge computing have a high degree of freedom and customization space.The trend of Hyper-Converged Infrastructure(HCI) in next generation data centers is expanding from Cloud to Edge. Traditional HCI systems provide software-defined unified solutions for computing, networking, and storage, and rely on virtualization. In the future, HCI will also integrate AI and Blockchain. A more efficient, flexible, and lightweight approach is preferred as the still limited resources at Edge when compared to Cloud. This proposal focus on rethink eBPF-based redesign and re-implementation of HCI at Edge for ARM + Linux, and comes with the following sub-topics:

1) eBPF-based In-Kernel services;

2) Ray and Redis based distributed scheduling, data processing and AI;

3) Kata containers, lightweight Kubernetes solutions like K3S & K2S, project Cilium, etc;

4) eBPF-centric new HCI solution for Edge computing.

The edge computing paradigm is becoming more and more popular, as the number of cloud workloads grows. While the most critical workloads continue running in the core, the less critical ones and those with strict requirements with regards to the latency and throughput are now being adopted in the edge. This means that instead of a small number of huge environments we are going to see a huge number of small environments during the following years.

But how do we scale out those clouds? Depending on the size of your organisation, there may be hundreds of them. Let's say there are five hundred edge clouds to be deployed in one year. This translates to almost two clouds per business day. How can one handle such a huge operational load?

During this presentation, we will demonstrate how can you quickly set up an OpenStack-based cloud by executing just six terminal commands. We will use MicroStack for this purpose. events.title: Cisco Container Platform - Self-healing, Scalable Kubernetes as a Service on Cisco Virtual Infrastructure Manager (CVIM)

But as more applications are moving to a microservices architecture, there is a need to extend CVIM to support hosting Kubernetes applications.  In this talk, we demonstrate how we deploy Cisco Container Platform on top of CVIM, with the objective of deploying numerous Kubernetes clusters on top of CVIM. We will also demonstrate how using our Control Plane, we perform lifecycle management and automated healing of the Kubernetes clusters. The Kubernetes clusters themselves are distributed and can auto-heal in the case of failures. What's more is you can use an edge compute host as a bastion into the edge network for deploying workloads as bare-metal instances,  where performance is crucial, such as video caching and streaming.

events.title: Are Your Secrets Secure?
events.body:
Whether you're following your own infosec policy or trying to meet the requirements of GDPR, ANSI, PCI DSS, HIPAA, or NIST you will want to answer the question: "Are my secrets secure?" in my OpenStack cloud.

Barbican is the OpenStack service that allows operators and users to store secrets securely.  It consists of an OpenStack API that provides keystone authentication, oslo policy and quotas, and back-ends in which the secret is actually stored.

But secrets are only as secure as the storage back-end that is deployed behind Barbican.

This talk will focus on the types of secure storage back-ends available, how they work, and the advantages and disadvantages of each back-end. We'll include discussion of HSMs, SGX and TPMs, and Vault.

The security of your secrets is important.  This session will give you the information you need to confidently make decisions about secret storage for your cloud.

events.body: Multiple types of servers are needed to handle diverse workloads. It allows customizing CPU core and frequency as well as a fine-grained control over CPU priority with Performance Base Frequency(PBF). It also allows setting the desired core count and their base and turbo frequencies which can help to tune the server to specific workload performance with Performance Profile (PP). Hence, one server can do more. In this session, we will talk about what these features are and how they can be helpful for cloud providers. We also talk about how the Intel SST is currently enabled in Nova and Ironic, with a preview of features that will be enabled in upcoming OpenStack releases.

events.title: Networking on steroids: Cyborg with NFV
events.body:
While SDN and NFV have brought the agility of software and the cost structure of COTS to networking, telcos are discovering that software-only approaches often fall short in key performance metrics such as latency, while consuming too much CPU, especially as we move to 100 Gbps and beyond.  Simultaneously, 5G and edge computing are driving a rapid evolution of networking standards and increased focus on power efficiency.

This talk will explain why these trends require programmable hardware accelerators for networking and how FPGAs fit the bill. We will explain the types of offload (from VNFs and from host infrastructure), major usage model (FPGA as a Service and Accelerated Functions as a Service) and some important NFV workloads (e.g. vRAN). We will explain why traditional OpenStack approaches are not adequate to handle FPGAs.  We will then present ways that OpenStack Cyborg can enable these new devices and trends in networking.
events.learning:
Attend this session to understand:

* The performance challenges posed by 100 Gbps, 5G and the Edge.

* Why these challenges require programmable network accelerators and smart NICs.

* How FPGAs fit the bill.

* The major usage models for network offload.

* The NFV/5G workloads that can benefit from hardware acceleration, such as vRAN  and BNG.

* Why traditional OpenStack approaches (SR-IOV with PCI whitelisting) are not a good fit.

* Cyborg's approach.

* Cyborg's status and future areas of work.

events.title: Efficient Monitoring and Root Cause Analysis in Complex Systems
events.body:
Real-life scenarios show that searching for the root causes of failures in complex systems can be very complicated and time consuming, leading, in the worst case, to lengthy outages. Therefore, operational real-time monitoring of the infrastructure is crucial to be able to quickly identify and alert on potential problems. But monitoring is not enough; when the failure occurs in a backend component such as memcached or database, configured alarms will typically cause an avalanche of notifications on all affected services and resources. A flexible mechanism for defining and analyzing relations between them is urgently needed.

In this presentation, we will show you how this can be achieved with Monasca and Vitrage, two OpenStack projects working together under the umbrella of the Self-Healing SIG. We will also refer to other possible integration points to implement fully automatic remediation.
events.learning:
In this presentation we demonstrate how Monasca and Vitrage can be efficiently used together to proactively detect problems and prevent possible outages.

Finally we show how the observability of OpenStack services and our solution can be improved by implementing Healthcheck APIs.

This project employs Akraino Integrated Cloud Native Edge Stack (ICN Blueprint) and Openstack StarlingX project separately to build an edge server which do remote graphical computing for client during gaming. The pixel information is calculated on edge server and sent to client. The edge server will run in a container environment to separate applications and make the whole system easy to deploy. 

Nowadays, cloud services are popular. These services are always built on a large group of servers to form a platform which provide virtual cloud machine to customers. It saves web companies' effort to build physical server network themselves, which reduce their cost and thus make a big market. Edge cloud, different from the cloud services mentioned above, is more geographically distributed and has much smaller scale. The technologies for edge cloud are developing, and people are also exploring its potential. Our sponsor, Intel, is working on developing edge cloud stacks. Intel is one of the key contributors to Akraino ICN, a blueprint for cloud native NFV and edge applications. They are also devoted to StarlingX, a fully integrated edge stack hosted in Openstack. In this project, we are going to employ edge cloud for low latency cloud gaming using Akraino ICN and StarlingX separately. As we know, some popular web games tend to require a lot on hardware (to do graphical computing) and less on internet speed. However, good equipment with high computational power is expensive and thus unnecessary for most people, while high internet speed is cheaper and cheaper. To solve it, we can run game on an edge cloud and send computed graph data to user. This will require low computational power and high internet speed. With fast and stable internet connection, cloud gaming will have a good performance on computation-required web games. What's more, compared to current cloud gaming services, the latency of edge cloud will be lower because of shorter geographical distance. This is edge cloud's advantage over current cloud, which makes it more suitable for cloud gaming.

1. Instance image from Nova side:

 Using nova image-create command, instance image can be created online and the file system will be frozen by Nova which will maintain the consistency of the data. However, the created image will depend on original system volume and snapshot.

2. Instance image from Cinder side:

Using cinder upload-to-image command, instance image can be created in qcow2 or raw format, which will be independent of original system volume. However, the image cannot be created online.

Those two images are applicable to different scenario:

1. The first method is applicable for user who has high demand of image creation speed and tends to maintain the original system and snapshot. 

2. The second method is applicable for user who wants to delete original system volume or snapshot.

events.title: OpenStack Momentum: What's Happening and Why It Matters
events.body:
OpenStack started life in 2010, driven by a small community of developers and users who saw opportunity in an open source cloud computing infrastructure project. The goal was simple: give everyone who wanted it the software to deploy and operate their own pool of compute, storage, and networking resources at scale, supported by a vendor or on your own if you wished.

Of course, things changed along the way. Public IaaS providers, powered by proprietary infrastructure, made big strides. New open source cloud technologies arose, offering equal parts capability and confusion. And, of course, everyone learned two hard truths: infrastructure is a big challenge, and so is maintaining a productive open source community

And so the OpenStack community responded. Powered by an agile and growing global community and a “four opens” model of how open source should work, the OpenStack community put forth a new roadmap, made hard choice, and refined its business models to reflect new realities. 

The results are beginning to speak for themselves. In the past year, a new momentum is building, driven by a focus on open infrastructure and a “four opens” philosophy focused on purposeful innovation. In this talk, we’ll talk about this journey and learn more about how the OpenStack community grew up and grew together to deliver new value for open infrastructure users and developers around the world.

events.body: There is a potential performance issue in every container-based platform. events.title: Kubinception: using Kubernetes to run Kubernetes at scale
events.body:
When faced with the challenge of building a managed Kubernetes service at OVH, fully based on open-source tools, we had to take some tough design decisions. One of them was rather structural: to deploy our customers' managed Kubernetes clusters over our own Kubernetes clusters. Kubinception indeed...

In this talk we will relate our experience running Kubernetes over Kubernetes for our managed Kubernetes service, with hundreds of customers' clusters. Why did we choose to build Kubernetes over Kubernetes? What are the main stakes when designing such an architecture? What problems did we encounter? How did we deal with theses issues? And, even more important, if we had to take the decision today, would we choose again to do the Kubinception?
events.learning: Our primary goal deploying our costumers' control planes on our admin clusters was efficiency, we wanted to deploy as much control planes in as few instances as possible. But we quickly realized we got a great side effect in terms of resilience and redundancy. And as added bonus, we could use the Kubernetes ecosystem to better operate our customer's clusters, for example by being able to monitor all our customers' control planes using K8s observability tools on our admin clusters. In the talk we intend to give a full disclosure of our solution, and of course we will also speak of the limits and drawbacks of this choice.

events.title: Avoiding obstacles on the river ride — from upstream to downstream CI
events.body:
When I joined Red Hat as a CI specialist, there were multiple definitions of what a "CI" system is.

My definition is simple: "A set of processes for continuously delivering 'verified' code supported by effective automated tooling"

The tools are the means and not an end unto themselves, but a very important means that can make our life easier.

At Red Hat we divide CI into Upstream, Midstream and Downstream. A simple division with many teams involved - without which you cannot sustain such a complex, constantly changing environment.

"Upstream" is self-explanatory. "Midstream" is the RPM-based RDO project. Finally, the downstream Red Hat OpenStack (RHOS) distribution is the tested and supported variant of RDO. RHOS has a much wider test matrix, with ~2200 CI jobs set, based on RHEL and TripleO running ... on Jenkins.

This presentation will show a real world example of adopting Upstream tooling via "Software Factory", for downstream RHOS product.
events.learning:
After this talk, the audience should get a clearer picture of why Upstream tools and definitions can't be 1-1 mapped to downstream CIs.  And the efforts (often underestimated) required to make the Upstream tooling fit into your Downstream environments—while not rippinng out the workflows your downstream teams are used to and cooperating with existing processes.

This talk will also help you understand why  proper planning and architecture for bringing cutting edge upstream tools to downstream CI ecosystem is crucial and can't be easilly  integrated without disturbing some of the existing workflows.

This session will help audience understand the growing trend that involves enterprise customers moving towards newer and more customizable and centralized privileged access management solutions. The open source community neither use these solutions, nor are cognizant of this. This session with touch upon how GDPR has changed the world from the way enterprises look at open source platforms and how there is a sudden need for communities like OpenStack to start looking at deployments and configurations from a new angle, that has non-open source elements like these PAM solutions. Inability for OpenStack to comply and co-exist with GDPR and such tools could mean enterprises could start considering other cloud solutions to achieve the same.

This session will not only talks about these challenges, it will also explain how these challenges were overcome and OpenStack was setup with one such tool.
